agents.name: claude
agents.description: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed.

agents.name: Explore
agents.description: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions.

agents.name: general-purpose
agents.description: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you.

agents.name: Plan
agents.description: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs.

agents.name: statusline-setup
agents.description: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting.

content.text:
Canada is the second-largest country in the world by total area, covering about 9.98 million square kilometres across the northern half of North America. It stretches from the Atlantic Ocean in the east to the Pacific in the west and up into the Arctic Ocean in the north, giving it the longest coastline of any country, roughly 243,000 km including its islands. Its only land neighbour is the United States, and the shared border, about 8,890 km long, is the longest international border in the world.

## Geography

Canada's landscape varies enormously from region to region:

- **The Canadian Shield** is an ancient expanse of Precambrian rock that covers nearly half the country, curving around Hudson Bay. It is dotted with countless lakes and holds large deposits of minerals such as nickel, gold, copper and iron.
- **The Western Cordillera** includes the Rocky Mountains and the Coast Mountains in British Columbia and Yukon. Mount Logan in Yukon is the highest peak at 5,959 m.
- **The Interior Plains**, which are the Prairies of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, are flat, fertile land that ranks among the world's great grain-producing regions.
- **The Great Lakes–St. Lawrence Lowlands** form the country's most densely populated and industrialized corridor, running from Windsor, Ontario, to Quebec City.
- **The Appalachian region** covers the Maritime provinces and eastern Quebec, with old, worn-down mountains and rugged coastlines.
- **The Arctic** consists of the vast Arctic Archipelago, including Baffin Island and Ellesmere Island, mostly tundra and ice.

Canada has more lakes than any other country, possibly more than half of the world's total. It also holds a large share of the world's fresh water. Major rivers include the St. Lawrence, the Mackenzie (the longest in Canada), the Fraser, the Yukon and the Nelson. The boreal forest that spans the country is one of the largest intact forest ecosystems on Earth.

## Climate

Most of Canada has cold winters, but climate varies widely by region. The coast of British Columbia is mild and wet, and Vancouver rarely sees prolonged snow. The Prairies have a continental climate, with very cold winters and hot summers. Southern Ontario and Quebec have humid summers and snowy winters. The Atlantic provinces have a maritime climate shaped by the ocean. The North has an Arctic climate with long, harsh winters and permafrost. Climate change is warming the Canadian Arctic at roughly two to three times the global average, which affects sea ice, permafrost and northern communities.

## Political Structure

Canada is a **federal parliamentary democracy** and a **constitutional monarchy**. King Charles III is head of state and is represented by the Governor General at the federal level and by Lieutenant Governors in the provinces. The head of government is the Prime Minister, who leads the party with the confidence of the elected House of Commons.

Parliament has three parts:
- **The Crown**
- **The Senate**, whose members are appointed on the Prime Minister's advice
- **The House of Commons**, made up of 343 Members of Parliament elected from ridings using a first-past-the-post system

The country has **10 provinces** and **3 territories**:

| Provinces | Territories |
|---|---|
| British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador | Yukon, Northwest Territories, Nunavut |

The provinces hold substantial constitutional powers over health care, education, natural resources and civil law. The territories exercise powers that the federal government delegates to them. The capital is **Ottawa**, Ontario.

The Constitution Act, 1982, brought the constitution fully under Canadian control and added the **Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms**. Quebec uses civil law, derived from the French tradition, for private matters. The rest of the country uses common law.

Major federal parties include the Liberal Party, the Conservative Party, the New Democratic Party (NDP), the Bloc Québécois, which runs candidates only in Quebec, and the Green Party.

## History

### Indigenous Peoples
People have lived in what is now Canada for at least 12,000 to 15,000 years, and likely longer. Indigenous Peoples, recognized constitutionally as **First Nations, Inuit and Métis**, developed diverse societies. Examples include the Haudenosaunee Confederacy around the Great Lakes, the Pacific Coast nations with their elaborate potlatch economies and totem-carving traditions, the Plains nations centred on bison, and the Inuit, who adapted to life in the Arctic.

### European Contact and Colonization
- Around **1000 CE**, Norse explorers briefly settled at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland.
- In **1497**, John Cabot reached the Atlantic coast while sailing for England.
- In **1534–1542**, Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence for France. The name "Canada" probably comes from the Huron-Iroquois word *kanata*, meaning "village" or "settlement."
- In **1608**, Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City, the beginning of New France.
- The **fur trade**, particularly beaver pelts, drove the colonial economy. The Hudson's Bay Company was chartered in 1670.
- In **1759**, the British defeated the French on the Plains of Abraham. The 1763 Treaty of Paris then transferred New France to Britain.
- The **Quebec Act of 1774** preserved French civil law and Catholic religious freedom.
- After the American Revolution, thousands of **United Empire Loyalists** moved north.
- In the **War of 1812**, British, Canadian and Indigenous forces repelled American invasions.

### Confederation and Expansion
On **July 1, 1867**, Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick united as the Dominion of Canada under the British North America Act, with Sir John A. Macdonald as the first Prime Minister. The country then grew:
- **1870**: Manitoba joined, along with the Northwest Territories, after the Red River Resistance led by Louis Riel.
- **1871**: British Columbia joined on the promise of a transcontinental railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway was completed in 1885.
- **1873**: Prince Edward Island joined.
- **1898**: Yukon became a territory during the Klondike Gold Rush.
- **1905**: Alberta and Saskatchewan became provinces.
- **1949**: Newfoundland joined.
- **1999**: Nunavut was created from the eastern Northwest Territories as an Inuit-majority territory.

### The 20th Century
- In **World War I**, Canada's victory at Vimy Ridge in 1917 became a defining national moment.
- The **Statute of Westminster (1931)** gave Canada legislative independence.
- In **World War II**, more than a million Canadians served, and Canadian forces landed at Juno Beach on D-Day.
- The post-war era brought the welfare state and universal health care. Saskatchewan's Tommy Douglas pioneered medicare, which became national by 1972.
- In the **1960s**, Quebec's Quiet Revolution brought rapid secularization and the rise of Quebec nationalism.
- In **1965**, Canada adopted the Maple Leaf flag.
- In **1969**, the Official Languages Act made English and French official languages.
- In **1971**, Canada adopted multiculturalism as official policy, the first country to do so.
- In **1980 and 1995**, Quebec held sovereignty referendums. The 1995 vote failed by a margin of less than 1%.

### Reconciliation
For over a century, the **residential school system** forcibly removed Indigenous children from their families in order to assimilate them. The last school closed in 1996. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which reported in 2015, called this "cultural genocide" and issued 94 Calls to Action. Reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples, including treaty rights, land claims, self-government and clean drinking water on reserves, remains a central national issue.

## Population and Demographics

Canada has about **41 million people**. Most live within roughly 160 km of the U.S. border. The largest metropolitan areas are:

1. **Toronto**, about 7 million, the financial and cultural centre
2. **Montreal**, about 4.5 million, the second-largest mainly French-speaking city in the world
3. **Vancouver**, about 3 million, the Pacific gateway
4. **Calgary** and **Edmonton**, each about 1.5 million or more
5. **Ottawa–Gatineau**, about 1.5 million

Canada has one of the highest immigration rates per capita in the world. About 23% of the population was born abroad. Large communities trace their origins to India, China, the Philippines, Pakistan, the Middle East, the Caribbean and Africa. Toronto and Vancouver rank among the most diverse cities in the world. In 2024–2025 the federal government reduced immigration and temporary resident targets in response to pressure on housing and services.

**Languages:** About 75% of Canadians speak English as their first official language and about 22% speak French. French is concentrated in Quebec, with significant communities in New Brunswick (Canada's only officially bilingual province), Ontario and Manitoba. Many Indigenous languages are spoken, including Cree, Inuktitut and Ojibwe.

## Economy

Canada has one of the largest economies in the world, with a GDP of about US$2.2 trillion. It is a member of the **G7**, the G20, the OECD, NATO and the Commonwealth. The main sectors are:

- **Natural resources**: Canada holds the world's third-largest proven oil reserves, mostly in Alberta's oil sands. It is also a leading producer of natural gas, uranium, potash, aluminium, nickel, gold and lumber.
- **Agriculture**: Canada is a major exporter of wheat, canola, lentils, pulses and beef.
- **Manufacturing**: Automotive production is concentrated in Ontario, alongside aerospace (Bombardier, CAE), machinery and food processing.
- **Services**: Services make up about 70% of GDP. Finance is dominated by the "Big Five" banks: RBC, TD, Scotiabank, BMO and CIBC. Technology hubs in Toronto, Waterloo, Montreal and Vancouver are known especially for AI research, building on the work of Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio.
- **Trade**: Roughly three-quarters of exports go to the United States. The trade relationship operates under CUSMA/USMCA. U.S. tariffs and trade tensions in 2025 strained relations and pushed Canada to diversify its trade and strengthen internal trade between provinces.

The currency is the **Canadian dollar** (CAD, the "loonie"), managed by the Bank of Canada.

## Social Programs

- **Universal health care (medicare)** is publicly funded and run by the provinces under the Canada Health Act. It is a strong part of national identity, although wait times are an ongoing concern.
- Canada also has public pensions (CPP/QPP and Old Age Security), employment insurance, the Canada Child Benefit, and newer national dental care and pharmacare programs.
- Education is a provincial responsibility. Canada ranks among the most highly educated countries in the world by share of adults with post-secondary education. Leading universities include the University of Toronto, McGill, UBC and Waterloo.

## Culture

- **Identity**: Canadian culture is often defined by its bilingualism, multiculturalism, Indigenous heritage, northern landscape, and contrast with the United States.
- **Sports**: Ice hockey is the national winter sport, and lacrosse is the national summer sport. The NHL has strong Canadian roots, and the Stanley Cup is a national obsession. Canada also invented basketball through James Naismith, and the Toronto Raptors won the NBA title in 2019. Curling and Canadian football (the CFL and the Grey Cup) are popular.
- **Music**: Notable musicians include Joni Mitchell, Leonard Cohen, Neil Young, Céline Dion, Shania Twain, Drake, The Weeknd, Justin Bieber, Arcade Fire, Rush and Alanis Morissette.
- **Literature**: Notable writers include Margaret Atwood, Alice Munro (Nobel Prize, 2013), Michael Ondaatje, Yann Martel, Lucy Maud Montgomery (*Anne of Green Gables*), Mordecai Richler and Gabrielle Roy.
- **Film and TV**: Notable figures include filmmakers Denis Villeneuve, David Cronenberg and James Cameron, along with a long line of comedians such as Jim Carrey, Mike Myers, the SCTV alumni and *Schitt's Creek*. Toronto and Vancouver are major production hubs nicknamed "Hollywood North."
- **Food**: Well-known foods include poutine, maple syrup (Quebec produces about 70% of the world's supply), butter tarts, Nanaimo bars, tourtière, Montreal-style bagels and smoked meat, bannock, peameal bacon, and Tim Hortons coffee.
- **Symbols**: National symbols include the maple leaf, the beaver, the Canada goose, the RCMP "Mounties," and the anthem "O Canada."

## Inventions and Contributions

Canadian inventions and contributions include insulin (Banting and Best, 1921), the telephone (partly developed by Alexander Graham Bell in Brantford), the snowmobile, the paint roller, the Canadarm, IMAX, the pacemaker, standard time zones (Sandford Fleming), the BlackBerry, and foundational work in deep learning.

## International Role

Canada pioneered modern **UN peacekeeping**. Lester B. Pearson won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1957 for helping resolve the Suez Crisis. Canada is a founding member of NATO and NORAD, is active in the Commonwealth and La Francophonie, and has a reputation for middle-power diplomacy, humanitarian work and resettling refugees. Arctic sovereignty, including the Northwest Passage, is a growing strategic priority as the ice retreats.

## Natural Wonders and Tourism

Popular attractions include Banff and Jasper National Parks in the Rockies, Niagara Falls, Old Quebec (a UNESCO World Heritage Site), the Cabot Trail in Nova Scotia, Gros Morne in Newfoundland, the Bay of Fundy (which has the world's highest tides), Haida Gwaii, the northern lights in Yukon and the Northwest Territories, polar bears at Churchill in Manitoba, and Vancouver Island's coastal rainforests.

---

**In summary**, Canada combines vast wilderness with highly urbanized, diverse cities. It is a stable, prosperous democracy shaped by Indigenous, French and British foundations and by waves of immigration from around the world. It is also still working through the legacy of colonialism and its relationship with its powerful southern neighbour.
